newsitem.title: USA: Opening statements key in Oklahoma bombing trial.
newsitem.headline: Opening statements key in Oklahoma bombing trial.

text.p: When the Oklahoma City bombing trial begins on Thursday, the prosecution will likely try to weave a compelling narrative for the 12 jurors to convince them that Timothy McVeigh was behind the deadly bombing.

The opening statement, to be presented by chief prosecutor Joseph Hartzler, will be a key opportunity for the government to lay out its case and suggest a broad theory that will later be fleshed out by the evidence.
McVeigh is accused of bombing the Alfred P. Murrah federal building on April 19, 1995, killing 168 people, including 19 children. He has pleaded not guilty and faces the death penalty if convicted.

"The prosecution can plant a compelling story in the jurors' minds," said Robert Precht, Director of the Office of Public Service of the University of Michigan Law School. He represented one of the defendants in the World Trade Centre bombing.

Jury and other psychological studies have shown that weaving a story is a powerful way to convey information, Precht said, because a story allows jurors to picture the events and digest the information presented.
People often retain information that fits the original story and reject anything that does not fit with what they have heard.

Prosecutors are expected to introduce handwriting samples and phone records allegedly linking McVeigh to the bombing and the purchase of the bomb's components. Traces of explosives were allegedly found on his clothing.
But for the defence, an opening statement presents a tricky challenge, Precht said.

The traditional theory was that the defence should entreat jurors to keep an open mind until all the evidence is presented. "But now the theory is that the defence should tell an alternate story -- just to keep its head above water," Precht said. "They need a narrative pull."

McVeigh's chief defence attorney, Stephen Jones, has already theorised that international "terrorists" may have been been behind the bombing that killed 168 people, including 19 children. He may also suggest that his client was framed.
One of the prosecution's key witnesses will be Michael Fortier, McVeigh's former friend, who is expected to testify that he knew McVeigh was planning the bombing but did nothing to stop him.

"Jones is going to have a field day with him," Precht said. Fortier has pleaded guilty to four felony accounts in return for testifying that he knew about McVeigh's plans to bomb the federal building but did not try to stop him. Fortier faces up to 23 years in prison.

Jones will be able to introduce for the jurors the idea that Fortier or even McVeigh's co-defendant, Terry Nichols, was responsible for the worst guerrilla attack on civilians. Nichols will be tried separately at a later date.

Also in the defence's arsenal is a recently released Justice Department report which disclosed that the famed FBI lab failed to follow proper procedures and drew unjustifiable conclusions in the case.
Prosecutors have said the report does not pose a threat to their case, but it worried Marsha Kight, whose 23-year-old daughter Frankie Merrell died in the April 19, 1995 blast, leaving a small child.
"There are things that might not be used because somebody didn't do their job right, and it was my daughter's life," Kight tearfully told reporters at the Denver courthouse this week.
